series: Things Living In Your House, Part 17
sources: Autumn et al. 2000, Nature, Adhesive force of a single gecko foot-hair; and Lewis & Clark College / UC Berkeley summaries: gecko toe pads carry millions of microscopic hairs (setae) that branch into hundreds of even finer tips (spatulae); they stick by van der Waals forces, dry, with no glue or suction; https://www.nature.com/articles/35015073

Smithsonian's National Zoo, Leopard gecko / gecko facts; San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, Lizards: most geckos have no movable eyelids, a clear scale covers the eye and the gecko licks it clean with its tongue; many lizards, including geckos, can drop the tail to escape a predator, the dropped tail keeps wriggling, and it grows back with cartilage instead of bone; https://animals.sandiegozoo.org/animals/lizard

University of Florida IFAS (Wildlife Ecology, Florida's introduced reptiles: Hemidactylus geckos), Common house gecko and Mediterranean house gecko: nocturnal, often seen on walls and around outdoor lights hunting insects attracted to the light; the common house gecko is native to Southeast Asia and has spread around the world with people and cargo; house geckos are harmless to people; they make chirping calls; https://edis.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/UW259

title: The Lizard on Your Ceiling Can't Blink, So It Licks Its Eyes 🦎
tiktok_caption: the lizard on my ceiling can't blink so it licks its own eyeballs 🦎 and its toes stick with no glue at all. Would you let one live in your house? 🦎 yes / 🚪 no

beats.say: That lizard on your ceiling can't blink. So it licks its eyeballs.
The house gecko. Out at night, on your walls.
It waits by your porch light.
Bugs fly to the light, and it snaps them up.
It has no eyelids, just a clear scale.
So it wipes its eyes with its tongue.
And it walks across the ceiling, no glue at all.
It's the cleanest-eyed roommate you've got.
